title: Pronoun Case and Sound-Alike Pronouns
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Grammar: Form, Structure and Sense
summary: Choose the right pronoun form — I or me, who or whom, its or it's, their, there or they're — with a quick test for every pair.

blocks.text: Pronoun **case** means the **form** a pronoun takes for its job in the sentence: *I* or *me*, *he* or *him*, *who* or *whom*, *its* or *it's*. Choosing the form has nothing to do with meaning — "Salma and me won" and "Salma and I won" mean the same thing — so the test uses these pairs to check whether you know the rules of Standard English. This lesson gives you a short test for every form, so you never have to guess by ear.
What this question type tests

These questions belong to **Standard English Conventions**, which is about **26%** of the scored Reading and Writing questions (about **11–15 questions** across the two modules). Inside that domain, the official skill group **Form, Structure, and Sense** covers pronoun use and the confusing sound-alike pairs that are named in the official skill list: **its/it's, their/they're/there** and **your/you're**. Convention questions **usually** come in the later part of each module, after Information and Ideas.
The stem is: **"Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?"** You know the question is about case or sound-alikes when the choices look like this:

items: I / me / myself / us
who / whom / which / whose
its / it's / its' / their
their / they're / there / its

blocks.text: The subject/object pairs (I/me, who/whom) are part of the same Standard English rules, and they often appear as wrong choices in pronoun questions, so learn them together with the sound-alikes.
Rule 1: Three forms — subject, object, possessive

headers: Object form (receives the action / after a preposition)

items: **Subject form** is used for the subject of a verb: "**She** designed the bridge." "**We** won."
**Object form** is used after an action verb and after a preposition: "The city hired **her**." "The prize went **to us**."
**Possessive** shows ownership and **never** takes an apostrophe: its, hers, ours, theirs, yours, whose. (*Her's*, *our's* and *its'* do not exist.)

blocks.text: Rule 2: Two people — cover the other one

The ear is usually right with one pronoun ("me won" sounds wrong) and usually wrong with two ("Salma and me won" sounds fine to many students). The fix is simple: **cover the other person** and test the pronoun alone.

rows: Salma and (I / me) won the debate.
The coach thanked Salma and (I / me).
(He / Him) and his sister run the shop.
The prize was shared by (she / her) and Karim.

items: **After prepositions** (between, for, with, to, from, among, like, except) always use the object form: ✓ **between you and me** · ✗ between you and I · ✓ **for him and her** · ✗ for he and she.
**We / us + noun:** drop the noun and test. "(We / Us) students asked for more time" → **We** asked → **We students**. "The talk was for (we / us) students" → for **us** → **us students**.

blocks.text: Rule 3: Comparisons with than and as
After *than* or *as*, the sentence is often unfinished. **Finish it in your head**, and the right form appears.

items: "Nour plays more expressively than (he / him)." → than **he** plays → ✓ **than he** / **than he does**.

"I trust Mona as much as (she / her)." Two meanings! → as much as **she** trusts Mona, or as much as I trust **her**. The passage decides; on the test, the choice with its verb ("she does") usually removes the doubt.
Choices like "than he does" are often the safest correct answers because the added verb makes the case obvious.

blocks.text: Rule 4: Myself, himself, themselves — only with a mirror

Reflexive pronouns (*myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves*) are correct only when the subject **acts on itself**, or for **emphasis** right after a noun. They cannot replace *I* or *me*.

items: ✓ I taught **myself** to code. (I … myself: the same person)
✓ The architect **herself** checked every beam. (emphasis)
✗ Karim and **myself** presented the project. → ✓ Karim and **I**
✗ Please send the files to **myself**. → ✓ to **me**
*Hisself* and *theirselves* are not words; the forms are **himself** and **themselves**.

blocks.title: غطّي الشخص التاني
blocks.text: لو الفراغ فيه شخصين (Salma and ___) **غطّي الاسم التاني** وجرّب الضمير لوحده: «I won» صح، «me won» غلط. وبعد الـ prepositions زي between / for / with دايمًا **me / him / her / us / them**. وكلمة **myself** متجيش غير لو نفس الشخص عمل الفعل لنفسه.
Rule 5: who, whom, whose, which, that

rows: a person, as the **subject** of its own clause (he/she/they)
the poet **who** wrote the anthem (she wrote it)
a person, as the **object** of its own clause (him/her/them), or after a preposition
the poet **whom** the committee honored (honored her) · the poet **to whom** it was dedicated
a writer **whose** novels … · a city **whose** streets flood easily
things and animals, **never** people; usually with commas (extra information)
people or things, in essential information (no commas)
the tool **that** they used · the doctor **that** treated him

blocks.text: **The he/him test:** take only the words of the small clause after the blank and put *he* or *him* in the gap. If **he** fits, use **who**; if **him** fits, use **whom**. Remember the *m*: hi**m** = who**m**.

items: "the engineer ______ the city hired" → the city hired **him** → **whom**
"the engineer ______ designed the bridge" → **he** designed the bridge → **who**
**Interrupter trap:** "the sculptor ______ historians believe made the bust" → remove *historians believe* → **he** made the bust → **who** (not *whom*).
**Preposition first:** after *to, with, for, by, of* + this word, always **whom**: "the scientist **with whom** she worked".
**which vs who:** a choice that uses *which* for a person is always wrong: ✗ "the teacher which helped me".

blocks.text: Rule 6: Sound-alikes — open the apostrophe

Possessive pronouns **never** have an apostrophe. An apostrophe in a pronoun always means a **contraction** (two words joined). So test every apostrophe by **opening it up**: if the long form makes sense, keep the apostrophe; if not, choose the possessive.

rows: a place, or "there is / there are"
Leave the boxes **there**. **There** are two exits.
belonging to whom / who is, who has

items: **its'** is never a word. Neither are *their's* or *your's*.
A possessive must be followed by a noun (or stand for one): "**their** keys". If the next word is a verb or an adjective ("______ able to"), you need a subject + verb: **they're** able to.
**There** can also start a sentence before a verb: "**There** are several reasons." It is never possessive.

blocks.title: الأبوستروف في الضمائر
blocks.text: لو لقيت **'** في ضمير يبقى معناه **اختصار** لكلمتين: it's = it is، they're = they are، you're = you are، who's = who is. الملكية في الضمائر **من غير** أبوستروف خالص: its, their, your, whose. افتح الاختصار في دماغك: لو الجملة باظت، يبقى الصح هو الملكية. وكلمة its' مش موجودة أصلًا.
The method for test day

items: **Read the choices.** Same pronoun in different forms (I/me, who/whom) or sound-alikes with and without an apostrophe?
**Apostrophe choices:** open each contraction (it is, they are, you are, who is). Does the sentence need a verb there? Then the contraction. Does a noun follow that is owned? Then the possessive.
**Subject or object?** Cover the other person; use the he/him test for who/whom; finish comparisons after than/as.
**People or things?** who/whom for people, which for things, whose for both.
**Check the number** too: their/they're must point to a plural noun; its/it's to a singular one.

blocks.text: Worked examples
Worked example 1: who vs whom

**Passage:** "The engineer ______ the city hired to design the new pedestrian bridge had already worked on several projects along the Nile Corniche. Her design, which uses lightweight steel cables, was chosen from more than forty proposals."
**Question:** Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

items: A) who
B) whom
C) which
D) whose

blocks.text: **Answer: B) whom.** Make the small sentence from the clause: "the city hired ___" → "the city hired **her**" (object form). Object form = "whom". The engineer receives the action of "hired"; "the city" is the subject of that verb.

items: **A) who** — "Who" is the subject form, but the subject of "hired" is "the city", not the engineer.
**C) which** — "Which" is used for things, never for a person.
**D) whose** — "Whose" shows possession: "whose the city hired" makes no sense.

blocks.text: Worked example 2: two people after a verb

**Passage:** "At the end of the season, the club's coach gave a short speech about teamwork. To everyone's surprise, she thanked my brother and ______ for staying late every evening to repair the old practice nets."
**Question:** Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

items: A) I
B) myself
C) me
D) mine

blocks.text: **Answer: C) me.** Cover "my brother and": "she thanked ___" → "she thanked **me**". After an action verb the object form is needed, so "my brother and me" is correct.

items: **A) I** — "I" is the subject form: "she thanked I" is wrong, even though "my brother and I" can sound polite.
**B) myself** — "Myself" is reflexive and needs "I" as the subject of the same clause; here the subject is "she".
**D) mine** — "Mine" is a possessive that stands alone ("the book is mine"); it cannot receive the action.

blocks.text: Worked example 3: they're vs their vs there

**Passage:** "Honeybees share the location of food through a movement called the waggle dance. When forager bees return to the hive, ______ able to show both the direction and the distance of a flower patch through the angle and length of their dance."
**Question:** Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

items: A) its
B) their
C) they're
D) there

blocks.text: **Answer: C) they're.** The clause needs a subject and a verb: "the forager bees **are** able to show". Open the contraction: "they're" = "they are", and "they" agrees with the plural "forager bees".

items: **A) its** — "Its" is possessive and singular; "its able" has no verb.
**B) their** — "Their" is possessive and must be followed by a noun; "their able" has no verb.
**D) there** — "There able" has no subject and no verb.

blocks.text: Worked example 4: whose vs who's

**Passage:** "Egyptian scientist Sameera Moussa, ______ research focused on the medical uses of nuclear physics, argued in the 1940s that atomic science should be used to treat disease and made as affordable as aspirin."
**Question:** Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

items: A) who's
B) whose
C) who
D) whom

blocks.text: **Answer: B) whose.** The clause shows possession: Sameera Moussa's research. Open the contraction in the trap choice — "who is research focused" is nonsense — so the possessive "whose" is correct.

items: **A) who's** — "Who's" means "who is" or "who has"; neither fits before "research".
**C) who** — "Who research focused …" has no possessive; it makes the woman the subject and leaves "research" without a role.
**D) whom** — "Whom" is an object form and does not show possession.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **"Me" vs "I" with two people:** cover the other person and test each pronoun alone.
**"Between you and I":** after a preposition it is always **me / him / her / us / them**.
**"Myself" for I or me:** only correct when the same person is the subject, or for emphasis.
**The interrupter:** "who historians believe made …" — remove "historians believe"; the pronoun is still a subject → **who**.
**"Which" for people:** always wrong; use who/whom/that.
**The apostrophe trap:** its, their, your, whose have **no** apostrophe; it's / they're / you're / who's are always two words; its' is never a word.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: See an apostrophe in a pronoun? Read it as two words. If that breaks the sentence, choose the possessive.
Ask: "Does the blank need a verb?" — a following adjective or -ing word ("___ able", "___ painted") means you need they're / it's / you're.
For who/whom, use the he/him test on the words of the small clause; for I/me, cover the other person.
After than/as, finish the sentence in your head.
Target time: about 25–35 seconds per question.

blocks.text: Practice
Ten original questions in Digital SAT format. Decide what job the pronoun does (subject, object or possessive) and open every apostrophe before choosing.

blocks.title: Pronoun case: practice quiz
blocks.intro: 10 original questions in Digital SAT format, untimed. Decide the pronoun's job first, and open every apostrophe.

questions.p: Ahmed Zewail, the Egyptian-American chemist ______ won the 1999 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, developed a method for observing chemical reactions as they happen, using extremely short flashes of laser light.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: He/him test: "___ won the prize" → "he won". Subject form = "who". "Whom" is the object form, "which" is not used for people, and "whose" shows possession.

questions.p: The archaeologist to ______ the discovery of the workers' village is usually credited spent nearly ten years mapping the site before the first houses were fully uncovered.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: After a preposition ("to"), the object form is needed: "credited to him" → "to whom". "Who" is the subject form, "which" is not for people, and "whose" needs a noun after it.

questions.p: During the robotics competition, my teammate Youssef and ______ were responsible for programming the robot's arm, while two other students built its wheels and battery case.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Cover "my teammate Youssef and": "___ were responsible" needs the subject form "I". "Me" and "us" are object forms, and "myself" cannot be a subject.

questions.p: Our grandfather left his collection of old family photographs to my sister and ______, and we have spent the summer scanning them so that the rest of the family can see them online.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: After the preposition "to", the object form is needed: cover "my sister and" → "left them to me". "I" and "we" are subject forms, and "myself" is reflexive, but the subject of "left" is "grandfather".

questions.p: The Nile crocodile can hold ______ breath underwater for more than half an hour, which allows it to wait unseen for prey close to the riverbank.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: A singular possessive is needed (the crocodile's breath), so "its" is correct. "It's" means "it is", "their" is plural, and "its'" is not a word.

questions.p: Many visitors are surprised by the colorful houses of the Nubian villages near Aswan. ______ painted in bright blues, yellows, and pinks, often with patterns of stars, birds, and palm trees.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The sentence needs a subject and a verb before "painted": "They are painted" (they = the houses). "They're" is correct. "Their" and "Its" are possessives with no noun to own, and "There painted" has no subject or verb.

questions.p: Naguib Mahfouz, ______ novels describe everyday life in the old neighborhoods of Cairo, became in 1988 the first Arabic-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The novels belong to Mahfouz, so the possessive "whose" is correct. Open "who's": "who is novels" makes no sense. "Who" and "whom" do not show possession.

questions.p: The sculptor Thutmose, ______ historians believe made the famous painted bust of Nefertiti, ran a large workshop in the city of Amarna, where the bust was found in 1912.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Remove the interrupter "historians believe": "___ made the famous bust" → "he made" → "who". "Whom" is the trap created by "historians believe"; "which" is not for people, and "whose" shows possession.

questions.p: Laila joined the debate club a year after her cousin, but according to their coach, she now speaks more confidently than ______ in front of the judges.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Finish the comparison: "she speaks more confidently than he does". The subject form with its verb is correct. "Him" is an object form, "himself" is reflexive, and "his" is a possessive with no noun.

questions.p: The museum's audio guide begins with a simple reminder for visitors: "When ______ standing in front of a statue, look closely at its base, where the name of the person it shows is often carved."
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The clause needs a subject and a verb before "standing": "When you are standing". "You're" = "you are". "Your" and "yours" are possessives, and "you standing" has no helping verb.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Subject form (I, he, she, we, they, who) does the action; object form (me, him, her, us, them, whom) receives it or follows a preposition.
Two people? Cover the other one. Comparison? Finish the sentence after than/as.
who/whom: he → who, him → whom; which is never for people; whose shows possession for people and things.
Possessive pronouns have **no apostrophe**: its, their, your, whose. it's, they're, you're, who's = two words.
Myself/himself only when the subject acts on itself or for emphasis.
